transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Oliver Grant (Vela CTO), Priya Rao (Vela ML Eng), Hannah Lee (Vela Infra)

Summary: quick scoping call to align on POC success criteria, workload sizing, reserved GPU commit vs burst, and fallback policies for the POC. Customer wants predictable latency under load and clear cost tradeoffs.

Topics: success criteria, qps/throughput, p95/p99 latency SLOs, reserved capacity sizing, burst strategy, fallback to smaller models, security/network requirements, POC timeline and benchmarks.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll keep this to about 50 minutes, quick intros  I'm Maya, AE on this deal, Liam is our SE who will own the benchmark plan.
[00:18] Oliver: Hi, Oliver here  CTO at Vela, thanks for the time. Main thing is we want to validate that Redwood can meet our latency SLOs with predictable costs for our chat assistant.
[00:28] Priya: Priya  ML Eng, I'll own the workload and provide prompts. We have a mix of short and long context.
[00:35] Liam: Great, quick note on what we'll cover: success criteria, what your peak QPS looks like, sequence lengths, caching opportunities, and then a proposed reserved GPU + burst plan for the POC.
[00:47] Hannah: I'm Hannah, infra lead  I'll handle networking and VPC stuff.
[00:52] Maya: Awesome. Oliver, can you run through the success criteria you mentioned?
[00:57] Oliver: Yeah so top-line: latency under 250ms median and p95 under 600ms for our real-time assist, cost target is roughly X per 1k requests  we don't have final unit pricing yet but we need to see ballpark. Also retention policy  logs can't leave EU for some users.
[01:22] Priya: Our workload: about 100k monthly active users, peak concurrency today around 120 concurrent chats, peak QPS for generation roughly 30 qps, but with bursty spikes up to about 80 qps during promotions. Sequence length distribution: 60% < 128 tokens, 30% 128-512, 10% >512. We do persistent chats so KV cache will matter.
[01:55] Liam: Good, that distribution helps  it'll influence batching and KV cache hit rates. For reserved capacity planning we usually size for baseline sustained qps and add burst credits for spikes. A typical POC uses reserved GPUs sized to cover baseline plus 20-30% buffer.
[02:12] Maya: Quick clarification  when Liam says reserved GPUs we mean dedicated capacity in Redwood Dedicated, right?
[02:17] Liam: Yes, Redwood Dedicated. For POCs, customers pick 1-2 reserved GPU nodes depending on model and throughput. We also offer burst credits to spill over to shared capacity or to additional dedicated instances temporarily.
[02:30] Oliver: What about fallback  if dedicated runs out, do we automatically route to hosted? Are there data residency or isolation issues?
[02:38] Liam: Good question. We support policy-based routing: prefer your dedicated pool, then fall back to hosted variants in the same region with optional data controls. For EU residency we can enable private deploy or VPC peering to keep traffic in region, but fallback to hosted may be restricted if you require strict on-prem residency. We'll note that.
[02:59] Priya: For the POC we can tolerate fallback to a slightly smaller model if latency spikes, as long as quality regression is small. We want to measure QA metrics though like answer relevance and hallucination rates across the model variants.
[03:17] Liam: That's exactly what we'll benchmark: baseline model (Vela's preferred open model), a quantized variant (int8) and a smaller fallback model. We'll measure throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, and output quality on your eval prompts.
[03:32] Maya: Oliver, do you have an internal timeline for the POC?
[03:36] Oliver: We're aiming for a 4-week POC, want a benchmark run in week 1, then a two-week customer evaluation, and final decision by end of month 4. So compressed.
[03:49] Maya: Ok, that'll work. We'll propose bench start next Monday.
[03:52] Hannah: Network constraints  we have strict egress controls; only a few IP ranges allowed and we need to see network diagram. Also SAML SSO is required for console access.
[04:05] Liam: We'll share the network diagram and SOC2 docs. SAML and RBAC supported. For VPC peering we'll collect CIDR ranges and port list.
[04:15] Priya: On workload traces  we can share 48 hours of traffic logs with token-level counts. We also have a set of 500 eval prompts we want used for quality metrics.
[04:25] Liam: Perfect. That will let us simulate a realistic QPS pattern and warm the KV cache to approximate hit rates.
[04:31] Oliver: Pricing  can you give a quick ballpark for reserved GPUs vs burst?
[04:35] Maya: Ballpark only today: a single A100-class reserved node for POC starts in the low X thousands per month, burst credits billed on consumption. We'll follow up with exact numbers; we'll also show cost per 1k requests estimates based on your token distribution.
[04:51] Priya: Do you have tooling to estimate cost per token for quantized vs non-quantized?
[04:55] Liam: Yes, Redwood Optimize provides model/quant recommendation and cost estimation; for example int8 quant can reduce per-token compute by ~30-40% for some models but may slightly increase latency variability. We'll include those numbers.
[05:09] Hannah: For the POC we want predictable p95s; variable latency spikes are a big concern. How does autoscaling avoid blips?
[05:16] Liam: Our autoscaler uses continuous batching and maintains warm KV caches; scaling decisions account for sequence length distribution and current KV usage. For sudden spikes we rely on burst capacity and temporarily route to compatible model variants to avoid cold-starts. We can also pin prewarmed instances during your peak window.
[05:34] Oliver: Can you quantify warm vs cold startup?
[05:37] Liam: Cold starts on large models can be several seconds, warm prewarmed instances reduce that to tens or hundreds of ms depending on kernel JIT and cache state. That's why reserved + prewarm is recommended for real-time apps.
[05:52] Priya: About eviction and fallback  if KV cache grows and we evict entries, does that materially affect latency?
[05:58] Liam: Eviction impacts quality more than latency; misses can increase compute per request but not necessarily long tails unless wallets warm caches. We'll measure local KV hit rates in bench runs.
[06:09] Maya: Let's get into sizing. Given 30 sustained qps baseline and 80 qps burst, with your token distributions, Liam, what nodes do you recommend?
[06:20] Liam: Quick back of envelope: baseline 30 qps with mixed sequence lengths  assuming 8 tokens/sec per concurrent stream and batching efficiency we estimate one A100-class GPU can handle ~40-60 qps for median workloads at p95 ~400-600ms. So baseline of 1 reserved node + burst capacity to handle spikes. For more headroom we'd recommend 2 nodes (one reserved, one as prewarm or burst). We'll run a bench to validate.
[06:52] Oliver: Hmm ok. What about a cheaper GPU class? We looked at T4s internally.
[06:57] Liam: T4s are cheaper but lower throughput and sometimes higher p99. For production SLOs we'd prefer A100 or H100 class; for exploratory sections T4 can be used. We'll include both options in the pricing.
[07:12] Priya: For the POC, could we start with 1 reserved A100 and enable burst credits to scale to 2-3 nodes during promos?
[07:18] Maya: Yes, that's a common pattern. You reserve the baseline and purchase burst credits or enable autoscale policies that spin extra nodes in the pool for limited time. Credits avoid surprise bills by setting caps.
[07:31] Hannah: On fallback policies  is it possible to fallback to a quantized variant of the same model in the same pool, instead of a different model?
[07:39] Liam: Yes, in many cases we can host multiple model variants and use model routing policies to fall back to a quantized variant first, then to a smaller architecture if needed. We'll measure quality delta during bench runs.
[07:52] Oliver: For evaluation we want to track both latency and a small set of quality metrics  BLEU isn't great for chat. We'll use human-annotated relevance and an LLM-based scoring metric.
[08:01] Priya: We'll share the eval rubric. Also we care about throughput for long contexts  >512 tokens  those are heavier.
[08:09] Liam: We'll run separate profiles for short, medium, long contexts to capture throughput and tail latency.
[08:15] Maya: Quick note on logs  do you need request/response logs to compute hallucination metrics?
[08:20] Priya: Yes  redacted logs are fine, but we need to keep them in EU.
[08:25] Liam: We can push bench logs to your S3 or to a temporary bucket in region; we'll also provide aggregated metrics in the console.
[08:34] Oliver: Ok sounds good. Can you confirm what the bench will look like?
[08:37] Liam: Bench plan (high-level): 1) Ingest workload traces and warm KV caches, 2) Run steady-state 2-hour tests at baseline qps, 3) Inject burst patterns to simulate promos (80-100 qps) for short windows, 4) Run model variant comparisons and collect quality metrics. We'll produce a benchmark report with p50/p95/p99 and cost estimates.
[09:00] Priya: Do you simulate cold starts too? We want to see worst-case tails.
[09:03] Liam: Yes, we'll include cold-start scenarios, and prewarm configs. We'll also test autoscale cooldowns to ensure we don't thrash.
[09:11] Hannah: Security checklist: SOC2, SAML, VPC peering, KMS integration for customer keys, audit logs retained 90 days.
[09:20] Maya: We'll attach the security pack and KMS integration docs.
[09:24] Oliver: Great. Any known limitations we should plan for?
[09:28] Liam: A couple: cross-region fallbacks may add latency; some quantized variants may slightly change tokenization edge cases; and if you require strict on-prem only we need a private deployment which is a bit longer to onboard.
[09:44] Priya: For quality gating, we want automated regression alerts if quality drops beyond threshold during the POC. Do you have that?
[09:50] Liam: Redwood Optimize has regression alerts tied to eval sets and can notify via webhook/Slack. We'll enable that for the POC.
[09:58] Maya: Let's recap the proposed POC footprint and next steps.
[10:02] Liam: Proposed: 1 reserved A100 node for baseline, burst credits to enable up to 2 additional nodes during spikes, prewarm policy during promos, model routing policy to fallback to int8 quant variant then smaller model, bench plan as described.
[10:19] Oliver: Sounds reasonable. We'll provide traces and eval prompts by 2026-04-01.
[10:24] Maya: We'll send a formal POC plan and pricing by 2026-04-02 and aim to start bench on 2026-04-06.
[10:32] Priya: On the bench data  do you need token-level timings or just counts?
[10:36] Liam: Token-level timing helps replicate real latency; counts are ok for rough sizing but timing is preferred.
[10:43] Hannah: We'll also email our networking constraints and allowed IP ranges.
[10:47] Maya: Anything else on the call?
[10:50] Oliver: One more thing  we may want a short demo of the Redwood console to see how to read the latency/cost breakdown.
[10:57] Maya: Happy to schedule a 30-minute demo next week  Liam can lead.
[11:02] Liam: I'll put together a short console walkthrough and the bench harness repo link.
[11:07] Priya: Cool. Thanks, everyone.
[11:09] Maya: Thanks all. Recap next steps and send notes.

End transcript.
